description: We are ASTRA-S (Astronaut Self-Tracking & Risk Assessment Software)
summary: ASTRA-S (Astronaut Health and Mission Monitoring System) is a dashboard that brings an astronaut’s health, sleep, activity, radiation, cabin environment, wellbeing and nutrition data into one mission-control view. Crews on long-duration missions are far from medical help. Chronic sleep loss, stress, radiation and drifting cabin conditions can build up unnoticed and wear down immune resilience and performance. ASTRA-S loads the mission’s sensor, survey and meal data and compares each reading with published reference ranges. It flags what needs attention and explains why, with supporting data and a suggested action to review with the crew medical team. Where the data can’t support a conclusion, it says so instead of guessing. The goal is to help crews and flight surgeons spot gradual changes early. ASTRA-S is a monitoring and decision-support aid, not a diagnostic tool.
details:
What it does and how it works

- ASTRA-S is a Streamlit web app with nine pages in a fixed sidebar:

- Mission Control gives an at-a-glance snapshot, trends, current alerts and a risk summary. Crew Profile covers three astronauts, with each person’s baselines.
Sleep covers duration, quality and sleep risks.

- Vitals & Activity covers heart rate, HRV, SpO₂, blood pressure, temperature, glucose and exercise. Radiation Watch shows the radiation readings. Crew Wellbeing has a self-report survey (loneliness, mood, stress, confinement, discomfort, mental exhaustion; 1 = worst, 10 = best). Cabin Environment covers oxygen, CO₂ and temperature. Nutrition Log is for logging meals. Risk Assessment brings every risk result together by category.

- CSV files are uploaded straight into the app and recognized by their columns, so nothing is hard-coded. A missing value shows “No Data”, not a made-up number.

- The Risk Diagnostics layer runs 15 assessments plus a sleep-quality score. Thresholds come from our team’s supplied Risk Assessment document and the references in it, such as American Heart Association blood-pressure categories and NASA-STD-3001 cabin limits. The sleep score weights duration, efficiency, interruptions and recovery. Each assessment reports a status (Urgent, Attention, Monitor, Optimal or Data limitation), supporting data, history, what may happen if the pattern continues, a recommended action, and its source. A correlation matrix helps screen for links between cabin conditions and health or wellbeing.

Benefits and intended impact

- It puts the signals that can affect immune health and wellbeing in one place, instead of nine separate tools.
- It spots slow trends, such as weeks of short sleep or repeated high resting readings, that a single reading would miss.
- It supports earlier, better-informed conversations between the astronaut and the medical team.
- It supports crew autonomy when ground contact is delayed.

Tools

- Python, Streamlit (interface), pandas and NumPy (analysis), Plotly (charts).
Matplotlib in Google Colab to prototype the risk analysis, and VS Code for development.
No special hardware. It runs on a laptop and reads CSV exports from wearable and cabin sensors.
- We tested it with sample data for three astronauts.

What is creative

- It is honest about uncertainty. It labels data limitations (for example, unknown fasting status for glucose, missing cabin pressure, or an undefined radiation unit) instead of forcing a verdict.
- It combines physiology, environment, behavior and nutrition in one system, and cross-checks them.
- It uses personal baselines (mean ± SD) rather than one-size-fits-all norms, and an astronaut-entered wellbeing check.
- It is modular: new risk modules plug in without redesigning the interface.

Factors we considered

- Safety and ethics: results are monitoring flags, not diagnoses. Medical and wellbeing information is shown only when authorized.
- Data quality: we handled missing values, mixed file formats, and the direction of the wellbeing scale.
- Reproducibility: the same data must always give the same result.
- Next steps: real-time sensor feeds, validation with clinical experts, and a switch to view each astronaut separately.
